background.title: Atoms, molecules and bonds
background.html:
Everything is made of tiny particles called atoms: carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S) are the ones in proteins. Atoms join into molecules.

  • Covalent bond: two atoms share electrons. Strong. It holds the atoms of one molecule together, drawn as a solid line, like C-N.
  • Hydrogen bond: a weak attraction between a slightly positive H and a slightly negative O or N nearby.
  • Ionic bond: the attraction between a positive and a negative charge.

Rule of thumb: strong covalent bonds build a chain; many weak bonds decide how the chain folds.

background.title: Charges, polar and non-polar
background.html:
Opposite charges (+ and −) attract; like charges push apart. A group of atoms is polar when it has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, for example −OH. Polar and charged groups are attracted to water: they are hydrophilic (water-loving).

Groups made only of carbon and hydrogen, such as −CH3, have no charged ends: they are non-polar and hydrophobic (water-hating). In water they cluster together, like oil drops.

background.title: Monomers, polymers, condensation and hydrolysis
background.html:
A polymer is a long chain of small repeating units, the monomers, like beads on a string. Proteins are polymers of amino acids; starch and glycogen are polymers of glucose.

A condensation reaction joins two monomers and releases a water molecule. Hydrolysis is the opposite: water is used to split the bond, as in digestion.

background.title: Chemical reactions, energy and catalysts
background.html:
In a chemical reaction, bonds break and new bonds form. The starting molecules are reactants (for an enzyme: the substrate); the new ones are products.

Every reaction needs a push of energy to get started, even one that releases energy overall, like a match that must be struck before it burns. A catalyst makes a reaction go faster without being used up. In living things the catalysts are enzymes, which are proteins.

background.title: Genes decide the order of amino acids
background.html:
A gene is a section of DNA. Its order of bases is a code for the order of amino acids in one polypeptide. The cell reads the gene and joins amino acids in that order at a ribosome.

So a change in the DNA (a mutation) can change one amino acid in the protein. You learn how the code is read in D1.2; today you only need: gene → order of amino acids → shape of the protein.

background.title: pH: acid, neutral, alkaline
background.html:
The pH scale runs from about 0 to 14. pH 7 is neutral (pure water); below 7 is acidic (stomach juice is about pH 2); above 7 is alkaline.

Acids contain many hydrogen ions, H+. Groups on a protein can pick up or lose H+, which changes their charge. That is why pH can change a protein's shape.

background.title: Rates, units and sketch graphs
background.html:
A rate is how much something changes per unit of time. In units, a power of −1 means "per": cm3 s−1 is read "cubic centimetres per second".

A sketch graph shows the shape of a relationship without exact numbers: rising, peaking, levelling off. The thing you change goes on the x-axis (across), the thing you measure on the y-axis (up).

Percentage change: (difference ÷ starting value) × 100.

terms.def: The small building blocks (monomers) of proteins. There are 20 kinds; a protein is a chain of them in a particular order.
A large molecule made of one or more chains of amino acids folded into a particular shape. Enzymes, insulin and collagen are proteins.
A large molecule made of many similar small units (monomers) joined in a chain, like beads on a string.
One of the small units that join in a chain to make a polymer.
The smallest particle of an element. Proteins are made of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur atoms.
A strong bond in which two atoms share electrons (tiny negative particles). It holds the atoms of a molecule together.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive H atom and a slightly negative O or N atom nearby. One is weak, but many together are strong.
An attraction between a positively charged group and a negatively charged group.
Electric charge is positive (+) or negative (−). Opposite charges attract; like charges push apart.
Having a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, like −OH. Polar groups are attracted to water.
Having no charged ends. Groups made only of carbon and hydrogen are non-polar, so water is not attracted to them.
"Water-loving": attracted to water. Polar and charged groups are hydrophilic.
"Water-hating": not attracted to water, so such groups cluster together away from it, like oil in water.
An acidic R-group can lose a hydrogen ion (H<sup>+</sup>) and become negative. A basic R-group can gain one and become positive.
A reaction that joins two molecules with a covalent bond and releases a molecule of water.
A reaction that uses a water molecule to split a covalent bond, breaking a large molecule into smaller ones. The opposite of condensation.
A chain of many amino acids joined by peptide bonds. A protein is one or more polypeptides, folded.
Two amino acids joined by one peptide bond.
To make a substance by building it from smaller ones. Protein synthesis is making proteins.
The rule by which the order of bases in DNA stands for the order of amino acids in a protein.
The order in which things come one after another, like letters in a word.
A change in the DNA of a gene. It can change one amino acid in the protein the gene codes for.
A protein is denatured when the bonds holding its 3D shape break, so it loses its shape and stops working. Usually permanent.
A scale of how acidic or alkaline a liquid is: 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline. Stomach juice is about pH 2.
The exact 3D shape of a protein.
An amino acid whose R-group contains sulfur (−SH). Two cysteines can join by a covalent disulfide bond.
The inside or centre of a folded protein, away from the surrounding water.
The very thin layer around a cell (and some structures inside it). Its middle is made of hydrophobic fatty tails.
A protein that sits inside a membrane, often crossing it from one side to the other.
Rounded and compact, like a ball. Globular proteins are usually soluble, for example enzymes and insulin.
Long and thin, like threads. Fibrous proteins are usually insoluble and strong, for example collagen.
Soluble: able to dissolve in water. Insoluble: does not dissolve.
A small protein hormone made in the pancreas. It travels in the blood and helps cells take up glucose, lowering blood sugar.
The red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. It has four chains, each with an iron-containing haem group.
A strong fibrous protein made of three chains wound together. It gives strength to skin, tendons, ligaments and bones.
A chemical messenger released into the blood that changes how certain target cells work.
A protein on or in a cell that a particular messenger molecule fits and binds to, which triggers a response.
A part of a protein that is not made of amino acids, such as the iron-containing haem in haemoglobin.
Tendons are tough cords joining muscles to bones. Ligaments join bones to other bones.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
A protein that speeds up one particular reaction in a living thing without being used up: a biological catalyst.
The molecule an enzyme acts on. It binds to the enzyme's active site and is changed into products.
The small pocket on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction happens.
All the chemical reactions going on in a living thing, linked to each other.
Reactions that build big molecules from small ones. They need energy.
Reactions that break big molecules into smaller ones. They release energy.
A very large molecule, such as a protein, starch or DNA, usually a polymer.
The store of glucose in animals (liver and muscles): a branched polymer of glucose.
The process in plants that uses light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
The process in every cell that releases energy from glucose. It is not the same as breathing.
Here: the removal of electrons (often with hydrogen) from a molecule, which releases energy, as in respiration.
Energy of movement. Warmer molecules have more kinetic energy, so they move faster.
To bump into each other. An enzyme can only act when a substrate molecule bumps into its active site.
The best value: the temperature or pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
An enzyme in most cells that splits hydrogen peroxide (a harmful substance) into water and oxygen.
An enzyme in saliva and the gut that digests starch into sugars.
The average: add the values and divide by how many there are.
The energy needed to start a reaction by breaking bonds in the substrate. Enzymes lower it.
Each enzyme acts on only one substrate (or a small group), because only that substrate fits its active site.
Fitting together as a matching pair, in shape and in charges.
The enzyme and its substrate while they are bound together, before the products leave.
Fixed in one place so it cannot move about.
Inside a cell. Extracellular means outside cells.
The first stage of respiration, in the cytoplasm: glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules.
A cycle of reactions in the mitochondria that continues breaking down the products of glycolysis in respiration.
A cycle of reactions in chloroplasts that builds sugar from carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.
Everything inside a cell's membrane except the nucleus: a watery fluid where many reactions happen.
Small structures in cells where most of the energy is released from food in respiration.
Makes again, so it can be used again.
A substance that slows down or stops an enzyme.
A binding site on an enzyme away from the active site. A molecule binding there changes the enzyme's shape.
Able to undo: a reversibly bound inhibitor can come off the enzyme again.
Medicines that lower blood cholesterol by blocking an enzyme in the liver that makes cholesterol.
A fatty substance made in the liver. Too much in the blood raises the risk of heart disease.
The final product of a chain of reactions.
An antibiotic: a medicine that kills bacteria by stopping them building their cell walls.
A stiff layer outside the membrane of bacteria (and plant cells) that stops the cell bursting.
Tiny single-celled living things with no nucleus. Some cause disease.
Here: bacteria are resistant when an antibiotic no longer kills them.
The molecule that carries genes: the instructions for making an organism's proteins.
IB command term: give a detailed account including reasons or causes. Say why or how, using "because" and "so".
IB command term: give a detailed account. Say what happens; reasons are not needed.
IB command term: give a brief account or summary.
IB command term: propose a solution, hypothesis or other possible answer, using what you know.
IB command term: make clear the differences between two or more things.
To look at two things side by side. In IB "compare and contrast": give similarities and differences, mentioning both things each time.
IB command term: work out a number answer, showing the steps of your working.
IB command term: draw a diagram or graph that shows the general shape, with labels, but not exact values.
IB command term: make a labelled, accurate diagram in pencil, with a ruler for straight lines.
